sections.introduction: Jerusalem artichokes are not true artichokes at all, but vigorous sunflower relatives grown for their knobbly underground tubers. They are hardy, reliable and useful for winter soups, stews and grated salads, with a sweet, nutty flavour which is not to everybody's taste and may not suit every digestion. The plants grow very tall in rich soil, making them useful as a screen or windbreak but also capable of robbing light from lower crops if planted in a long row. They are easy to grow from tubers, but hard to eradicate once established because even small pieces left in the soil can regrow.

soil_facts.text: Light, sandy or free-draining soil suits the crop, provided it is not very acid or waterlogged in winter. Improve heavy clay before planting.
Prepare in autumn or early winter, removing perennial weeds and adding compost or well-rotted manure where humus is low. Sandy soil needs less preparation, though compost can improve the crop.

looking_after_the_crop.text: Hoe between young plants or mulch deeply to suppress weeds, particularly on heavy ground. Established plants on light soil usually need little attention.

text.metric: Earth up the bases when stems are about 30 cm tall. Water during dry weather, especially on light soil.
text.imperial: Earth up the bases when stems are about 1 ft tall. Water during dry weather, especially on light soil.

looking_after_the_crop.text: In windy sites, put sturdy canes at the ends of the row and run supporting wires along both sides. Tall stems can also make a temporary windbreak.
Remove flower buds if desired and give weak plants an appropriate organic liquid feed during summer.

text.metric: Once autumn leaves turn brown, cut stems to about 30 cm above the soil. Healthy tops can be reused as mulch or woven into a temporary windbreak.
text.imperial: Once autumn leaves turn brown, cut stems to about 1 ft above the soil. Healthy tops can be reused as mulch or woven into a temporary windbreak.

harvesting.text: Lift tubers as needed from late autumn through early spring. They are hardy, but frozen ground can prevent access: lift a supply before a hard freeze.
Reserve sound tubers for replanting. Remove unwanted tubers and fragments carefully because even small pieces can regrow.
When clearing a bed, revisit it through spring and repeatedly remove shoots and their tubers. One lifting may not clear the crop completely.

final_tips.text: Keep the tall plants north of shorter vegetables so the screen does not rob them of light.
A manageable clump is often easier to accommodate than a long shading row.
In severe frost, cover stem bases with straw or lift tubers after the tops have died back.
Protect stored tubers from rodents and inspect them regularly for damage or decay.

soil_facts.text: Choose a sunny, sheltered site with rich, moist but well-drained soil. Improve heavy clay and avoid winter waterlogging.
Prepare deeply with compost or well-rotted manure. Test before liming towards pH 6.5; mulch to conserve moisture.

looking_after_the_crop.text: Water deeply until established and during drought, especially as heads form. Mulch and weed; an organic feed after the first heads can support further growth.
Remove old woody stems and yellow leaves after cropping. Retain three or four strong new shoots.
In cold areas protect crowns with loose straw or leaves. Loosen covers in mild wet weather to prevent stagnant damp.

harvesting.text: Pick young, tight, tender heads before the scales open and become woody or prickly.
Cut the main head first with a short stalk, then take smaller side heads as they develop. A second flush may follow in a long, mild season.
Remove early heads from weak first-year plants to build strength for later cropping.

final_tips.text: Seed-raised plants vary; offsets from good plants give more dependable results.
Replace ageing crowns gradually with vigorous suckers instead of renewing the whole bed at once.
Very young heads may be eaten almost whole; older heads yield the fleshy scale bases and heart.
Inspect winter protection after wet weather and keep crowns out of stagnant damp.

sections.introduction: Aubergines are decorative, heat-loving relatives of the tomato, grown for their glossy fruits as well as their purple flowers and large velvety leaves. They can crop well under glass or in a warm polytunnel, but outdoors they are a gamble except in very warm, sheltered places. The key requirement is heat: cool, grey weather slows growth and often delays fruiting until late summer. Treat aubergines as tender annuals, give them rich soil, steady moisture without waterlogging, and harvest the fruits while the skin still has its shine. Fruits may be oval, round or long, and varieties range from the familiar dark purple to white, violet and striped forms.

looking_after_the_crop.text: Keep warm and water according to growth: less in cool weather, more in heat, without waterlogging. Ventilate to avoid stagnant dampness.
Stake and loosely tie stems to keep fruit off the soil. Pinch tips if the variety needs bushier growth; thin excess young fruit only if larger fruit are wanted.
Use an organic potassium-rich feed once fruits swell. Inspect leaves for mites and whitefly so biological control can start early.

harvesting.text: Cut glossy fruit at a useful size instead of pulling. Do not wait until skins dull, fruit swell across the middle or seeds harden.
Regular picking encourages more fruit into early autumn, until cold nights slow growth.
At the end of the season, chop or shred healthy woody stems before composting.

harvesting.text: Pick green leaves for summer salads as needed. Cut non-forcing heads in autumn; use promptly or keep cool, and protect crops left standing from frost.

Check dark covers for slugs or rot without leaving the shoots exposed to light.

sections.introduction: Florence fennel, or bulb fennel, is a sweet, aniseed-flavoured umbellifer grown for the swollen bases of its leaf-stalks. It belongs to the same broad family as carrot, parsnip and celeriac, but is eaten quite differently: sliced raw in salads, cooked gently for a soft creamy flavour, or used in soups and ratatouille. The feathery leaves are also edible, with a mild dill-like flavour. Modern varieties have made it easier to grow by reducing the tendency to bolt before useful bulbs form. Match the variety to its sowing season and keep young plants growing steadily: drought, crowding or root checks can give stemmy plants instead of juicy bulbs. Summer sowings after an early crop are useful for autumn harvesting. Harvest while the bulbs are tender, before they become fibrous, stemmy or frosted.

sections.introduction: Leeks are among the most dependable alliums for a home garden, carrying the harvest from late summer through winter and, with the right varieties, into spring. They quietly gain size while summer crops fade, then provide sweet white shanks and useful green leaves when few fresh vegetables are available. Although closely related to onions, they are generally easier and more tolerant, especially in cool, moist conditions, but they still need a long season, steady moisture, transplanting and some attention to blanching. Their flavour is at its best in cool, cloudy weather and through the hungry gap, when winter and spring varieties such as Musselburgh, Bandit, Apollo or St Victor can be especially welcome. Choose varieties to match the season: fast summer and autumn leeks for early lifting, hardier shorter-stemmed sorts for winter, and late varieties that keep cropping into April or May before flower stems begin to form.

sections.introduction: There is something especially exciting about the sight of the first flush of mushrooms breaking through the surface. Mushrooms are fungi rather than vegetables, but they are an obvious choice for a gardener with spare indoor space, because they need no direct sunlight and can be grown when outside beds are quiet. Growing them can be unpredictable: outdoor planting is a gamble, and home-made compost takes considerable preparation. For small quantities, fresh ready-spawned button-mushroom compost is the simplest and most predictable route. Follow the supplier’s instructions for the particular kit, as other mushroom species need different substrates and conditions. Healthy spent compost can be used in the garden after the final crop.

sections.introduction: Onions and shallots are among the most useful crops in the kitchen garden, providing fresh bulbs, salads, pickles and winter stores. Spring-planted sets offer a simple start; seed gives a wider choice of colours, sizes and seasonal types. Shallot bulbs usually divide into clusters, while overwintered onions provide earlier harvests. All need clean, fertile ground and careful drying for storage, but differ in timing and bolting risk.

looking_after_the_crop.text: Mulch annually with compost or well-rotted manure, keeping the central crown clear.

final_tips.text: Forced stalks are earlier, paler and milder, but forcing weakens the crown: give it a rest the following year.
Healthy crown divisions retain a named variety; seedlings take longer and may vary.
Divide an ageing or crowded crown during dormancy and retain vigorous healthy pieces.
Leaves are not edible. Compost them and use only the stalks in the kitchen.

sections.introduction: Spinach is a quick leafy crop which can be available for much of the year with careful planning, but it needs steady moisture and rich soil to avoid bolting. There are summer and winter forms of true spinach, while New Zealand spinach is a separate, frost-tender plant often grown as a summer substitute in hot weather. Perpetual spinach, or spinach beet, is a type of leaf beet rather than true spinach. Choose the appropriate type for the season and pick tender leaves regularly.

sections.introduction: Tomato plants are found in the majority of greenhouses during summer, producing a succession of fruit from early summer into autumn. They need constant care: water growing bags or pots regularly in summer and watch for pests and diseases. Home growers can choose flavours and varieties that are rarely sold commercially. Tall or cordon plants are trained with one central stem and their side-shoots removed throughout the season. They need warmth, light, steady root moisture, good ventilation and balanced fertility more than sheer feeding.

sections.introduction: Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.
